issue: Own-prose "emoluments" (STYLE-NOTE: use pay/compensation; "emolument" only in Constitution quotations). Source: "a greater number of offices and emoluments will flow"; candidate: "More offices and emoluments will flow from their gift."
replacement: Many considerations, in addition to those I suggested on a former occasion, seem to put it beyond doubt that the people's first and most natural attachment will be to the governments of their own States. More individuals will expect to rise into the administration of these governments. More offices, with the pay attached to them, will flow from their gift. Their watchful care will regulate and provide for all the more domestic and personal interests of the people. The people will know their affairs more familiarly and in more detail. And a greater share of the people will have ties of personal acquaintance and friendship, and of family and party attachment, with their members. The popular bias may well be expected to lean most strongly toward these governments.

issue: Weakened claim. Source: "our past experience is very far from countenancing an opinion" (i.e. gives no support); candidate: "gives very little support to the opinion" (implies some support).
replacement: Examine the new Constitution accurately and fairly, and you will find that the change it proposes consists much less in adding NEW POWERS to the Union than in strengthening its ORIGINAL POWERS. The regulation of commerce, it is true, is a new power. But few oppose this addition, and no one fears anything from it. The powers concerning war and peace, armies and fleets, treaties and finance, and the other more considerable powers, are all vested in the existing Congress by the Articles of Confederation. The proposed change does not enlarge these powers; it only substitutes a more effective way of administering them. The change concerning taxation may be regarded as the most important. Yet the present Congress has as complete authority to REQUIRE indefinite supplies of money from the States, for the common defense and general welfare, as the future Congress will have to require them from individual citizens. And the citizens will be no more bound than the States themselves have been to pay the quotas assessed on each of them. Suppose the States had complied punctually with the Articles of Confederation, or suppose their compliance could have been enforced by means as peaceable as can be used successfully on single persons. Our past experience gives no support to the opinion that the State governments would then have lost their constitutional powers and gradually been entirely consolidated. To maintain that such a result would have followed would be to say outright that the existence of the State governments is incompatible with any system whatever that accomplishes the essential purposes of the Union.

issue: Source: "Notwithstanding the want of proper sympathy in every instance between the local sovereigns and the people"; candidate: "did not always have the sympathy of the people" (changes "in every instance" to "not always").
replacement: The feudal system showed a similar tendency. The local sovereigns lacked the proper sympathy of the people in every instance, and in some instances the general sovereign had it. Even so, it usually happened that the local sovereigns won the rivalry in encroachments. If external dangers had not forced internal harmony and subordination, and especially if the local sovereigns had held the people's affections, the great kingdoms of Europe would today consist of as many independent princes as they once had feudal barons.

issue: Source: "as has been elsewhere remarked" (passive, unattributed); candidate: "as I have remarked elsewhere" invents authorship by the speaker.
replacement: Suppose, then, that the people should in future become more biased toward the federal government than toward the State governments, as has been remarked elsewhere. The change could only result from such manifest and irresistible proofs of better administration as would overcome all their earlier inclinations. In that case the people surely ought not to be barred from giving most of their confidence where they find it most deserved. And even then the State governments would have little to fear, because, by the nature of things, federal power can be administered to advantage only within a certain sphere.

issue: Emphasis capital dropped. Source: "The SIXTH and last class"; candidate: "The sixth and last class" (STYLE-NOTE: keep emphasis capitals; only the paragraph-opening word is normalized).
replacement: The SIXTH and last class consists of the various powers and provisions that give effect to all the rest.

issue: Ungrammatical/awkward: "Congress has never been able, and cannot be able, to carry out" for source "has been or can be executed by Congress".
replacement: Suppose the Convention had taken the first course and adopted the second article of the Confederation. Then the new Congress, like its predecessors, would constantly face a choice between two alternatives. It could read the word "EXPRESSLY" so strictly that the government was left with no real authority at all, or so loosely that the restriction lost all its force. It would be easy to show, if it were necessary, that Congress has never been able, and never will be able, to carry out any important power delegated by the Articles of Confederation without turning, more or less, to the doctrine of CONSTRUCTION or IMPLICATION. The powers delegated under the new system are more extensive, so the government administering it would be still more hard pressed by the alternative of betraying the public interests by doing nothing, or violating the Constitution by exercising powers that are indispensably necessary and proper but not EXPRESSLY granted.

issue: Modal/term drift: source "must give pleasure to every citizen" -> candidate "should be pleased"; source "the necessity of denying" -> "the reasons for denying" (drops "necessity"); source "the intercourse among them" -> "trade among them" (narrows).
replacement: Every citizen must be pleased that the prohibition now reaches bills of credit, in proportion to his love of justice and his knowledge of the true sources of public prosperity. Since the peace, America has suffered from the pestilent effects of paper money on the confidence needed between man and man, on the confidence needed in the public councils, on the industry and morals of the people, and on the character of republican government. These losses are an enormous debt, chargeable against the States that adopted this unwise measure, and it must long remain unpaid. Or rather, they are an accumulated guilt that can be expiated only by one thing: a voluntary sacrifice, on the altar of justice, of the very power that has been the instrument of it. Beyond these persuasive considerations, we may observe that the necessity of denying the States the power of regulating coin prove equally that they should not be free to put a paper medium in the place of coin. If every State had a right to regulate the value of its coin, there might be as many currencies as there are States, and dealings among them would be obstructed. Its value could be altered retroactively, which would injure the citizens of other States and kindle animosities among the States themselves. Subjects of foreign powers might suffer in the same way, and so the Union would be discredited and drawn into quarrels by the indiscretion of a single member. A power in the States to emit paper money is no less open to every one of these harms than a power to coin gold or silver. The power to make anything but gold and silver a tender in payment of debts is withdrawn from the States on the same principle as the power to issue a paper currency.

issue: Fixed-term collision and overstated claim. Source: "instead of considering in the first place what degree of power was absolutely necessary ... have exhausted themselves in a secondary inquiry"; candidate: "never stopped to ask first ... spent all their energy" ("never" is stronger than "instead of"; "energy" is a fixed term with a different sense).
replacement: The opponents of the Convention's plan, instead of first asking how much power the federal government absolutely needs for its purposes, have exhausted themselves on a secondary question: what the proposed degree of power might do to the governments of the particular States. But consider what has been shown. The Union is essential to the security of the American people against foreign danger. It is essential to their security against quarrels and wars among the different States. It is essential to protect them from those violent and oppressive factions which embitter the blessings of liberty, and from those military establishments which must gradually poison liberty at its very fountain. In a word, the Union is essential to the happiness of the American people. Given all this, is it not preposterous to object to a government, one without which the objects of the Union cannot be attained, that it may diminish the importance of the governments of the individual States? Was the American Revolution fought, was the American Confederacy formed, was the precious blood of thousands shed and the hard-earned wealth of millions spent, so that the people of America might enjoy peace, liberty, and safety? Or was it so that the governments of the individual States, those particular municipal establishments, might hold a certain extent of power and be dressed in certain dignities and attributes of sovereignty? We have heard of the impious doctrine of the Old World that the people were made for kings, not kings for the people. Is the same doctrine now to be revived in the New World in another shape, so that the solid happiness of the people is to be sacrificed to the views of political institutions of a different form? It is too early for politicians to count on our having forgotten this: the public good, the real welfare of the great body of the people, is the supreme object to be pursued, and no form of government has any value except as it is fitted to attain that object. If the plan of the Convention were against the public happiness, my voice would be, Reject the plan. If the Union itself were inconsistent with the public happiness, it would be, Abolish the Union. In the same way, wherever the sovereignty of the States cannot be reconciled with the happiness of the people, the voice of every good citizen must be, Let the former be sacrificed to the latter. How far the sacrifice is necessary has been shown. How far what remains unsacrificed will be endangered is the question now before us.

issue: Source: "the immediate dependence of the one on the other" (one-directional; developed in the next paragraph: federal on State); candidate: "how directly each depends on the other" makes it mutual.
replacement: The State governments will have the advantage over the federal government by whatever measure we compare them: how directly the one depends on the other; how much personal influence each side will have; what powers each is given; which the people prefer and are likely to support; and how willing and able each is to resist and frustrate the other's measures.

issue: Fixed-term drift: STYLE-NOTE renders "the several departments" as "the separate departments"; candidate keeps "The several departments of power".
replacement: One of the main objections pressed by the more respectable opponents of the Constitution is that it supposedly violates the political maxim that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments ought to be separate and distinct. In building the federal government, they say, no heed seems to have been given to this essential precaution in favor of liberty. The separate departments of power are, they say, distributed and blended in a way that at once destroys all symmetry and beauty of form, and exposes some of the essential parts of the edifice to being crushed by the disproportionate weight of the others.

issue: Fixed-term drift: "the several departments of power have been kept absolutely separate and distinct" (STYLE-NOTE: several -> separate/individual).
replacement: Look at the constitutions of the individual States. The axiom has been laid down emphatically and, in some of them, in unqualified terms. Yet in not one State have the individual departments of power been kept absolutely separate and distinct. New Hampshire, whose constitution was the most recently formed, seems to have recognized fully that avoiding any mixture of these departments whatever is both impossible and unwise. She has qualified the doctrine by declaring "that the legislative, executive, and judiciary powers ought to be kept as separate from, and independent of, each other AS THE NATURE OF A FREE GOVERNMENT WILL ADMIT; OR AS IS CONSISTENT WITH THAT CHAIN OF CONNECTION THAT BINDS THE WHOLE FABRIC OF THE CONSTITUTION IN ONE INDISSOLUBLE BOND OF UNITY AND AMITY." Her constitution accordingly mixes the departments in several ways. The Senate, a branch of the legislative department, also sits as a judicial court to try impeachments. The President, who heads the executive department, also presides over the Senate, where he has an equal vote in all cases and a casting vote in a tie. The executive head is himself elected each year, in the final stage, by the legislative department, and his council is chosen each year by that department from among its own members. Several officers of state are also appointed by the legislature. And the members of the judiciary department are appointed by the executive department.

issue: Fixed-term drift: "the several departments" (STYLE-NOTE: -> separate).
replacement: The conclusion I am warranted in drawing from these observations is that merely marking the constitutional limits of the separate departments on parchment is not a sufficient guard against those encroachments which lead to a tyrannical concentration of all the powers of government in the same hands.

issue: Force strengthened. Source: "it appears that the constitution had been flagrantly violated by the legislature"; candidate: "They show that the legislature had flagrantly violated the constitution".
replacement: The other State I shall use as an example is Pennsylvania, and the other authority is the Council of Censors, which met in 1783 and 1784. Part of this body's duty, as the constitution laid it out, was "to inquire whether the constitution had been preserved inviolate in every part; and whether the legislative and executive branches of government had performed their duty as guardians of the people, or assumed to themselves, or exercised, other or greater powers than they are entitled to by the constitution." In carrying out this trust, the council had necessarily to compare the proceedings of both the legislature and the executive with these departments' constitutional powers. The facts the council set out were mostly accepted as true by both sides in it. It appears from them that the legislature had flagrantly violated the constitution in a variety of important instances.

issue: Source: "a very ineffectual capacity in the latter to defend itself"; candidate "proved quite unable" is stronger than "very ineffectual".
replacement: In every example of ancient and modern confederacies, we have seen the members showing the strongest tendency to strip the general government of its authorities, while the general government was very ineffectual at defending itself against their encroachments. Most of these systems were so unlike the one before us that any inference from their fate to ours is greatly weakened. Still, the States will keep a very large share of active sovereignty under the proposed Constitution, so the inference should not be dismissed entirely. In the Achaean league, the federal head probably had a degree and kind of power that made it much like the government framed by the Convention. The Lycian Confederacy, as far as its principles and form have been handed down, must have resembled it more closely still. Yet history never tells us that either of them degenerated, or tended to degenerate, into a single consolidated government. We know, on the contrary, that one of them was ruined because the federal authority could not prevent the quarrels, and finally the disunion, of the subordinate authorities. These cases deserve our attention all the more because the outside pressures forcing the component parts together were far more numerous and powerful than in our case. Weaker bonds within would therefore have been enough to hold the members to the head and to each other.

issue: Added "us" (not in source).
replacement: The Confederation left the right of coining money in the hands of the States, which this clause now takes from them. They held it alongside Congress, subject to one exception: Congress alone had the right to regulate the alloy and value. Here, too, the new provision improves on the old. So long as the general authority fixed the alloy and value, a right of coinage in the particular States could do nothing except multiply expensive mints and vary the forms and weights of the coins in circulation. That second problem defeats one of the purposes for which the power was first given to the federal head. The first might spare the inconvenience of shipping gold and silver to a central mint for recoinage, but local mints established under the general authority can serve that end just as well.

issue: "paper emissions" is archaic/opaque to a general reader; keeps source phrase otherwise.
replacement: Experience says the same. The federal administration has so far been very defective compared with what may be hoped for under a better system. Yet during the war, and especially while the independent fund of paper-money issues was in credit, it had as much activity and importance as it can well have in any future circumstances. It was also engaged in a course of measures aimed at protecting everything dear to the people at large and winning everything they could desire. It was nevertheless invariably found, once the passing enthusiasm for the early Congresses was over, that the people's attention and attachment turned back to their own particular governments. The federal council was never the idol of popular favor. And the side usually taken, against proposed enlargements of its powers and importance, was that of the men who wished to build their own political consequence on their fellow citizens' prepossessions.

issue: Added framing sentence "Consider what the supposition demands." (no counterpart in source; STYLE-NOTE: no additions).
replacement: The only refuge left to those who prophesy the downfall of the State governments is the visionary supposition that the federal government may first build up a military force for the projects of ambition. The reasonings in these papers must have been employed to little purpose indeed if I must now disprove the reality of this danger. The people and the States would have to elect, for a long enough time, an unbroken succession of men ready to betray both. Throughout this time the traitors would have to pursue, uniformly and systematically, some fixed plan for extending the military establishment. And the governments and the people of the States would have to watch the gathering storm silently and patiently, and keep supplying the materials, until it was ready to burst on their own heads. To everyone this must seem more like the incoherent dreams of a delirious jealousy, or the misjudged exaggerations of a counterfeit zeal, than like the sober apprehensions of genuine patriotism. Extravagant as the supposition is, however, let it be made. Let a regular army fully equal to the resources of the country be formed, and let it be entirely at the devotion of the federal government. Even so, it would not be going too far to say that the State governments, with the people on their side, would be able to repel the danger. By the best computation, a standing army in any country cannot be raised above one hundredth part of the whole number of souls, or one twenty-fifth part of the number able to bear arms. In the United States that proportion would produce an army of no more than twenty-five or thirty thousand men. Against these would stand a militia of nearly half a million citizens with arms in their hands, officered by men chosen from among themselves, fighting for their common liberties, and united and led by governments that possess their affections and confidence. It may well be doubted whether a militia in such circumstances could ever be conquered by so small a proportion of regular troops. Those who know best how this country recently and successfully resisted the British arms will be the most inclined to deny the possibility. The Americans have the advantage of being armed, which they hold over the people of almost every other nation. Beyond that, there are the subordinate governments to which the people are attached and which appoint the militia officers. These form a barrier against the enterprises of ambition more insurmountable than any that a simple government of any form can offer. The several kingdoms of Europe carry their military establishments as far as the public resources will bear, and yet their governments are afraid to trust the people with arms. And it is not certain that, with arms alone, the people would fail to shake off their yokes. But suppose the people had the further advantages of local governments chosen by themselves, able to collect the national will and direct the national force, and of officers appointed out of the militia by these governments and attached both to them and to the militia. It may be affirmed with the greatest assurance that the throne of every tyranny in Europe would be quickly overturned in spite of the legions that surround it. Let us not insult the free and gallant citizens of America with the suspicion that they would be less able to defend the rights they actually possess than the debased subjects of arbitrary power would be to rescue theirs from their oppressors. Let us rather stop insulting them with the supposition that they can ever bring themselves to the necessity of making the experiment, through blind and tame submission to the long train of insidious measures that must precede and produce it.

issue: Source: "the general mass of power"; candidate "the whole mass" changes the qualifier.
replacement: We have reviewed the general form of the proposed government and the general mass of power allotted to it. Now I turn to the particular structure of this government and to the way that mass of power is divided among its constituent parts.

issue: Added "show something more" (not in source); the clause "to show that unless ..." should stay one construction.
replacement: The last paper showed that the political saying examined there does not require the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments to be wholly unconnected with each other. Now I shall undertake to show that, unless these departments are connected and blended enough to give each a constitutional control over the others, the degree of separation that the maxim requires as essential to a free government can never in practice be properly maintained.

issue: Added "right to" (source: "The constitutional trial by jury had been violated").
replacement: The constitutional trial by jury had been violated, and powers had been taken that the constitution had not delegated.

issue: Source: "including even justices of the peace and sheriffs"; candidate "down to" drops "including even" (and repeats "down to").
replacement: In South Carolina, the constitution makes the executive office elective by the legislative department. It also gives the legislative department the appointment of the members of the judiciary department, including even justices of the peace and sheriffs, and the appointment of officers in the executive department, down to captains in the army and navy of the State.
